stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 11.1 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 307 K and 1.05 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 35.0 mL of 0.15 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.2 M NaOH.
2.4 g of $$\ce{KNO3}$$ dissolves in 138 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 7.9 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e- -> Cu}$$ E° = 0.34 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Mg (Z = 12) and Al (Z = 13) are compared.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 125 g of $$\ce{NaCl}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 58.44 g/mol.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 47. What is K for the reaction multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.02 M solution of $$\ce{KOH}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 1 × 0.02 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 31 L flask at 1.67 atm and 344 K?
Samples of $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: H2 2.02, Cl2 70.9, Ar 40, CO2 44.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.07 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 890 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A 29 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 27.3 mL of 0.261 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 8.1. In a solution at pH 10.8, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 7.3. In a solution at pH 6, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 78 kJ/mol, the transition state at 137 kJ/mol and the products at 11 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 59, ΔH = -67, reverse Ea = 126 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.52 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (0.96).

questions.stem: A 25.6 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 41.9 mL of 0.259 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: The nitrate ion has three resonance structures. What is true of its N–O bonds?

options.text: One is double and two are single at all times
They alternate rapidly between single and double
All three are identical, intermediate between single and double bonds

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of chlorine (Cl, Z = 17)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 17 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 2 × 10⁻¹². At equilibrium:

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal

questions.stem: Which formula is most likely for the compound of element X (Group 2) and element Y (Group 16)?
A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0117 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
What is the oxidation number of S in $$\ce{SO4^{2-}}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.5 mol N₂, 0.7 mol O₂ and 0.1 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.5 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{NO3^-}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas deviate most from ideal behavior?

options.why: Correct. Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.explanation: Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 9.6. A mixture has [A] = 0.7 M, [B] = 0.5 M and [C] = 0.4 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.457
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.457
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.457, which is less than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 1.14

questions.stem: If ΔH = −286 kJ for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), what is ΔH for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂ + O₂?
What is the mass percent of O in $$\ce{C6H12O6}$$?

options.why: Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
There are 6 atoms of O in the formula.
That is the percent of the other elements.

questions.stem: 45 mL of 0.17 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.1 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$$, 45 g of $$\ce{CH4}$$ reacts with 15 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 17 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -6.86; K = 1.05 \times 10^{-3}. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.1 mol N₂, 0.4 mol O₂ and 0.8 mol Ar at a total pressure of 2.3 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{NaF}$$ or $$\ce{CaO}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{NaF}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{NaF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ is consumed at 0.82 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{H2O}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 6/5.

questions.stem: In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
198 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 67 g of water at 28 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.052 mol of solute in enough water to make 464 mL of solution?
What volume does 1.4 mol of gas occupy at 1.58 atm and 330 K?

options.why: Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.
22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.529 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 661 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
For a reaction, ΔH° = -164 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 44 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 565 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.2 M solution of hypochlorous acid (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-8})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.2 M and [I₂] = 2 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.66 M. What is K?
The Ksp of $$\ce{PbI2}$$ is 7.1 \times 10^{-9}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
A photoelectron spectrum shows 6 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 : 2. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}\,4s^{2}$$, which has 20 electrons.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -405 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -309 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 805, 1521, 2540, 12700 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 3 electrons, so it has 3 valence electrons.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.1 mol N₂, 0.1 mol O₂ and 0.3 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.4 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: F is less electronegative than I
The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: What is the hybridization of the central atom in $$\ce{CH2O}$$?

options.why: Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Correct. Hybridization matches the number of electron domains: 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.

questions.explanation: CH2O has 3 electron domains on the central atom.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 13 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -5.25; K = 5.26 \times 10^{-3}. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O(g)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.25 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.2) and 0.08 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 2 electrons transferred and E° = 0.12 V.
ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.2) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 128 mL. What is the pH after 63.8 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.072 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 59 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 9.2 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 2270 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
Divide by the moles of reactant.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{Mg(OH)2}$$ is 5.6 \times 10^{-12}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$$.

options.why: Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.129 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.05 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Al.
Explain why the 1s peak of Al has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Mg.

rubric.criterion: Al has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Al has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Mg: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
